title: Querying Data with SQL
summary: Learn to extract and analyze data from relational databases using SQL. This lesson covers filtering and aggregations, the major join types, subqueries and CTEs, and window functions for advanced analytics tasks data scientists face daily.
objectives: Write SELECT queries that filter, group, and aggregate data to answer analytical questions
Combine tables correctly using INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL joins
Use subqueries and common table expressions (CTEs) to structure complex logic
Apply window functions for running totals, rankings, and period-over-period comparisons
Understand SQL logical execution order to debug queries and avoid common mistakes

quiz.q: Which clause filters rows AFTER aggregation has occurred?
quiz.why: WHERE filters rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the aggregated results after GROUP BY runs.

quiz.q: You want to keep all customers even those with no orders. Which join should you use (customers on the left)?
quiz.why: A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table (customers) and fills NULLs where there is no matching order.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a window function from a GROUP BY aggregation?
options: Window functions collapse rows into one
Window functions compute across rows without collapsing them
Window functions cannot use ORDER BY
quiz.why: Window functions perform calculations over a set of related rows while preserving each individual row, unlike GROUP BY which collapses rows into summaries.

quiz.q: In SQL's logical execution order, which clause is evaluated first?
quiz.why: SQL logically begins with FROM to identify the source data, then applies WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, and finally ORDER BY.

quiz.q: Name the keyword used to define a Common Table Expression (CTE).
quiz.why: CTEs are introduced with the WITH keyword, which names a reusable, readable result set used in the main query.

quiz.q: Which window function would you use to compare each row's value to the previous row within a partition?
quiz.why: LAG accesses a value from a prior row in the ordered window, ideal for period-over-period comparisons. LEAD does the same for the next row.

body_markdown:
## Why SQL for Data Scientists

Most real-world data lives in relational databases. Before you can model or visualize anything in Python, you need to pull the right data. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the universal tool for querying relational data, and fluency in it separates productive data scientists from those who wait on engineering teams.

## The Core Query Structure

A basic query follows a familiar pattern:

```sql
SELECT column_a, column_b
FROM table_name
WHERE condition
GROUP BY column_a
HAVING aggregate_condition
ORDER BY column_b
LIMIT 100;
```

**Logical execution order** differs from the written order. SQL evaluates clauses roughly as: `FROM` -> `WHERE` -> `GROUP BY` -> `HAVING` -> `SELECT` -> `ORDER BY` -> `LIMIT`. This is why you cannot reference a `SELECT` alias inside a `WHERE` clause, but you can in `ORDER BY`.

## Aggregations

Aggregate functions collapse many rows into a summary value: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`. Pair them with `GROUP BY` to compute per-group summaries.

```sql
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS num_orders, AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
FROM orders
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
```

Use `WHERE` to filter rows *before* aggregation and `HAVING` to filter *after* aggregation.

## Joins

Joins combine rows from multiple tables based on a related key.

- **INNER JOIN**: only rows with matches in both tables.
- **LEFT JOIN**: all rows from the left table, NULLs where no match on the right.
- **RIGHT JOIN**: all rows from the right table.
- **FULL OUTER JOIN**: all rows from both, matched where possible.

```sql
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

A LEFT JOIN is your friend when you want to keep all customers even those without orders (great for spotting churn or gaps).

## Subqueries and CTEs

A **subquery** is a query nested inside another. A **CTE** (Common Table Expression) using `WITH` makes complex logic readable and reusable.

```sql
WITH high_value AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000
)
SELECT c.customer_name, h.total
FROM high_value h
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = h.customer_id;
```

Prefer CTEs over deeply nested subqueries for readability and easier debugging.

## Window Functions

Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row **without collapsing them** like `GROUP BY` does. The `OVER()` clause defines the window.

```sql
SELECT
    order_date,
    amount,
    SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS order_seq,
    LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_amount
FROM orders;
```

Common window functions: `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, `DENSE_RANK`, `LAG`, `LEAD`, and aggregate functions with `OVER`. `PARTITION BY` resets the window per group; `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` defines ordering for running/ranking calculations.

## Practical Tips

- Always inspect a sample with `LIMIT` before running heavy aggregations.
- Be explicit with table aliases when joining.
- Watch for fan-out: joining one-to-many can inflate aggregate counts.
- NULLs do not match in joins or equality; handle them deliberately.

slides.title: Querying Data with SQL
slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll learn how to query relational databases with SQL, the everyday tool data scientists use to extract data before any analysis or modeling begins. We'll cover aggregations, joins, subqueries, CTEs, and window functions.

slides.title: Why SQL Matters
bullets: Most production data lives in relational databases
SQL is the universal query language across systems
Pull the right data before modeling in Python
Fluency means independence from engineering teams
slides.narration: Before you can train a model or build a dashboard, you need the right data, and most of that data sits in relational databases. SQL is the universal language for accessing it. Being fluent in SQL lets you answer questions on your own instead of waiting on others, which makes you far more productive as a data scientist.

slides.title: Query Structure & Execution Order
bullets: Written: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
Logical order: FROM then WHERE then GROUP BY then HAVING then SELECT then ORDER BY
Can't use SELECT aliases in WHERE
Can use them in ORDER BY
slides.code:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM orders
WHERE amount > 0
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY n DESC;
slides.narration: A query is written in one order but executed in another. SQL starts with FROM, then filters with WHERE, groups, applies HAVING, then evaluates SELECT, and finally orders and limits. This explains a common confusion: you can't reference a SELECT alias in WHERE because WHERE runs first, but you can in ORDER BY which runs later.

slides.title: Aggregations
bullets: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX collapse rows
GROUP BY computes per-group summaries
WHERE filters before aggregation
HAVING filters after aggregation
slides.code:
SELECT category, AVG(amount) AS avg_amt
FROM orders
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
slides.narration: Aggregate functions summarize many rows into a single value. Combine them with GROUP BY to get per-group results, like average order amount per category. Remember the key distinction: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the grouped results after aggregation.

slides.title: Joins
bullets: INNER: only matching rows in both tables
LEFT: all left rows, NULLs when no match
RIGHT: all right rows
FULL OUTER: everything, matched where possible
slides.code:
SELECT c.customer_name, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
slides.narration: Joins combine rows from multiple tables on a shared key. INNER JOIN keeps only matches; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills NULLs where there's no match. Use a LEFT JOIN when you want to keep all customers, including those with no orders, which is perfect for finding gaps or churn.

slides.title: Subqueries & CTEs
bullets: Subquery: a query nested inside another
CTE with WITH names a reusable result set
CTEs improve readability and debugging
Prefer CTEs over deeply nested subqueries
slides.narration: When logic gets complex, subqueries let you nest one query inside another. Common Table Expressions, written with the WITH keyword, give that subquery a name and make your code read top to bottom. For anything beyond trivial nesting, prefer CTEs: they're easier to read, test, and debug.

slides.title: Window Functions
bullets: Calculate across rows without collapsing them
OVER() defines the window
PARTITION BY groups; ORDER BY orders within window
ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, running SUM
slides.code:
SELECT order_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total,
  LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                    ORDER BY order_date) AS prev
FROM orders;
slides.narration: Window functions are the superpower for analytics. Unlike GROUP BY, they compute across related rows while keeping every row intact. The OVER clause defines the window: PARTITION BY resets per group, and ORDER BY sets the sequence for running totals or rankings. Functions like ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, and LEAD enable rankings and period-over-period comparisons.

slides.title: Practical Tips
bullets: Inspect samples with LIMIT before heavy queries
Use explicit table aliases when joining
Beware fan-out from one-to-many joins inflating counts
NULLs never match in equality or joins
slides.narration: A few habits will save you pain. Always preview data with LIMIT first. Use clear table aliases in joins. Watch out for fan-out, where a one-to-many join multiplies rows and inflates your aggregates. And remember NULLs don't match anything in equality comparisons, so handle them deliberately. With these fundamentals you can confidently extract data for any analysis.
